newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - December 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Ireland - December 9.

text.p: Following are the highlights of stories reported in the Irish press on Monday.

- The controversial Price Waterhouse report, believed to include details of payments by Dunnes Stores to political figures, is expected to be given to Judge Gerard Buchanan, a retired judge of the Circuit Court, around midday on Monday.
- The murder of Peter Judge, one of Dublin's main drug dealers, may generate another spate of gangland violence.
- The British Prime Minister John Major has said he "will not wait for too long" before deciding whether any new IRA ceasfire "is going to be sustainable".
- Police are investigating claims of sexual abuse at one of the state's largest institutions for orphans and boys with mental handicap.
- Pay talks between the government, unions and employers resume on Monday with emphasis switching to the public service.

- Wall Sreet may have recovered from an early 140 point loss last Friday to close less than one percent down on the day, but the reverberations from what has been dubbed "Wobbly Friday" means that both bond and equity markets will open nervously on Monday.
- There will be no IRA ceasefire this Christmas, republican sources in Dublin and Belfast said on Sunday.
- Soaring revenue returns and a 25,000 reduction in dole numbers will give Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn enough scope in his January budget for a major election year tax package.
- Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams on Sunday dismissed remarks by British Prime Minister John Major on the possibility of a renewed IRA ceasefire and the entry of republicans into all party talks.
- Irish Prime Minister John Bruton will try on Monday to keep alive the possibility of a deal on an IRA ceasefire that would bring Sinn Fein into round-table negotiations.
- The Irish Prime Minister John Bruton and three of his ministers have admitted that they received election funding from Ben Dunne and Dunnes Stores in the past.

- Despite appearances, Ireland's budgetary position is one of the worst in the EU and a long way off what will be required to meet the likely regime in a single European currency, Davy Stockbrokers chief economist O'Leary has said.
